sentences.text: Stethacanthus was an extinct genus of shark-like cartilaginous fish that died out around 298.9 million years ago.
This fish holds the record for the first known large mass of globular calcified cartilage in chondrichthyans.
The elaborate spine-brush complex appears only in sexually mature males.
Small spikes covered the anvil-shaped crest and the shark's head.
The genus Stethacanthus was first described by Newberry in 1889.
Species discovered in the late 1800s were initially identified based only on isolated spines, confusing Newberry into thinking they were a new type of fin.
The family Stethacanthidae was defined by Richard Lund in 1974 due to the distinct differences of Stethacanthus from other elasmobranchs.
Stethacanthus fossils have been found in New Mexico approximately 360 million years ago.
Stethacanthus was a carnivore that likely fed on brachiopods and crinoid ossicles.
Researchers suggest that Stethacanthus likely fed on other small fish species.
Stethacanthus was probably a slow-moving shark due to the drag force produced by its large spine-brush complex.
Stethacanthus may have been a bottom-dweller based on its small fins and teeth relative to other Paleozoic sharks.
Stethacanthus may have been migratory, as many specimens were found in the Bear Gulch Limestone, a potential breeding ground.
It is suggested that the fin whips were used during mating, though their exact purpose is unknown.
Researchers suggest the crest may have been used for mating rituals, clamping onto larger animals, or frightening predators.
It is debated whether the crest served a function in courtship or was used for defense.
Stethacanthus is classified within the class Chondrichthyes.
Stethacanthus belongs to the superorder Selachimorpha.
Stethacanthus is classified in the extinct order Symmoriida.
Stethacanthus belongs to the family Stethacanthidae.
The type species of the genus Stethacanthus is Stethacanthus altonensis.
Several species of Stethacanthus have been described, including S. mirabilis, S. praecursor, S. productus, S. thomasi, and S. gansuensis.
Stethacanthus lived from the Late Devonian to the Late Carboniferous.
Fossils of Stethacanthus have been found in Australia, Asia, Europe, and North America.
New discoveries have expanded the known range of Stethacanthus to Scotland, Central Russia, and China.
Zangerl hypothesized that the spine-brush complex may have been inflatable, similar to human erectile tissues.
Theories suggest the spine-brush complex and head denticles were used to scare predators by simulating a larger fish's mouth.
The classification of symmoriids relative to stethacanthids remains a subject of debate.
